title: The Divided Self: An Existential Study in Sanity and Madness
author: R.D. Laing
edition_analyzed: Penguin Modern Classics edition (most commonly cited, content substantially unchanged from original)
target_audience: Readers interested in the nature of self and consciousness
People affected by or interested in psychosis and schizophrenia
General readers interested in the human mind and radical psychology
core_themes: The experience of self-division in psychosis
Interpersonal relationships and the ontological security of the self
Existential approaches to understanding mental illness
Empathy and subjectivity in the therapeutic relationship
primary_purpose: To explore the nature of madness and sanity through an existential lens, arguing that psychosis can be understood as a crisis of selfhood and interpersonal relationships, and advocating for a more humane, empathetic approach to treatment that acknowledges patients' subjective experiences.

structure_format.narrative_style: Analytical yet accessible; combines philosophical discourse with clinical observation and case studies
structure_format.organization: Begins with philosophical groundwork on selfhood, then details clinical case studies and theoretical discussion of schizophrenia and psychosis
features: Case studies of individuals experiencing schizophrenia

key_concepts_lessons: Schizophrenia and psychosis can be interpreted as profound divisions within the self, rather than just biomedical disorders.
The 'ontologically secure' person feels unified and real, whereas the 'ontologically insecure' person experiences profound self-alienation.
Understanding and compassion are essential in psychotherapy; it is imperative to see the world from the patient's perspective.
Standard psychiatric approaches may depersonalize and alienate those suffering from mental illness.
The experience and expression of insanity are deeply influenced by one's relationships and existential anxieties.
notable_features: Groundbreaking use of existential-phenomenological analysis in mental health
Radically humanistic perspective for its time
cultural_historical_context: Published at the cusp of the 1960s, during a period of upheaval in psychiatry and psychology (emergence of anti-psychiatry, existentialism). Reacted against dehumanizing trends in institutional psychiatry and played a central role in the humanistic mental health movement.
reception_impact: Widely influential in psychiatry, psychology, and philosophy
Sparked debate over the nature and treatment of mental illness
Foundational work in the anti-psychiatry movement and humanistic therapy
Ongoing source of inspiration and controversy in mental health debates
Still referenced in discussions of the subjective experience of madness
comparable_titles: Madness and Civilization by Michel Foucault
Psychiatry and the Human Condition by R.D. Hinshelwood
Being and Nothingness by Jean-Paul Sartre
Sanity, Madness and the Family by R.D. Laing and Aaron Esterson
One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest by Ken Kesey (fiction, but thematically resonant)
